name: Kalighat Painting Workshop
description: KALIGHAT PAINTINGS – WHERE TRADITION MEETS MODERNITYBengal is renowned for its rich cultural heritage and diverse artistic traditions, including music, literature, dance, and visual arts. In this workshop, we will explore one of Bengal's most fascinating and thought-provoking art forms—Kalighat Paintings.Bold, expressive & vibrant, Kalighat paintings beautifully bring together a variety of themes, ranging from Hindu mythology and spirituality to secular life and social commentary.Originating in 19th-century Kolkata during the colonial period, this distinctive art form developed around the Kalighat Temple, dedicated to Goddess Kali. The paintings were traditionally created on patas (cloth or paper scrolls) by artists known as Patuas. Located near the banks of the Hooghly River and the popular Kalighat Temple, the area attracted pilgrims, locals, and foreign visitors, creating a thriving audience for these unique artworks.However, with the growing popularity of printed reproductions in the early 20th century, traditional handmade Kalighat paintings gradually declined.The legacy of this expressive art form was later reinterpreted and celebrated by renowned Indian artist Jamini Roy, who drew inspiration from Bengal's folk traditions and brought a distinctive modern interpretation to traditional Indian art.What will you learn?Learn about the history and evolution of Kalighat PaintingsExplore the life and artistic journey of Jamini RoyUnderstand the distinctive themes, styles, and visual language of this art formDiscover how traditional Indian folk art influenced modern artistic expressionCreate your very own Kalighat-inspired paintingThis will be a wonderful opportunity to experience Indian art and culture through storytelling, learning, and hands-on creativity!Note:All art materials required for the workshop will be provided by the host.What will you take home?A Detailed Hands-On Workshop WorkbookKnowledge & History of Kalighat art & cultureYour very own completed artwork created during the workshopWhat do you need to bring?A water bottle to keep yourself hydrated.All workshop materials will be provided. description: An afternoon on the one conversation you keep putting off.What We'll DoYou'll arrive with one conversation you've been avoiding - with a co-founder, a parent, a manager, a client, anyone. name: शून्य शिखर - Shoonya Shikhar
description: In Sanskrit, shoonya is the word for zero. Indian mathematicians gave it a place among the numbers, and long before that, and alongside it, the word meant emptiness. Kabir and the Nath yogis before him used a form of it, sunn, for the still centre a seeker reaches when the mind's chatter falls away. It is not a blank. It is what remains when there is nothing further to add.Most concerts climb towards a peak. This one goes the other way. Each song will be a little quieter than the one before, and the evening will end closer to silence than to applause.Vedanth Bharadwaj and Gurupriya Atreya begin. They start with the Bhakti poets, songs that still have some movement and argument in them, and then turn gradually towards gentler pieces, the kind that ask the room to lean in rather than sit back.Mir Rajak and Group follow, Mirasi musicians from Pugal in Rajasthan, whose families have sung the Sufiyana kalam for generations. Their music is often full-throated, built for courtyards and long nights. Tonight they sing Kabir, Bulleh Shah and other Sufi poets in its softer, more inward register, the way these songs are sung when the gathering is small and no one is in a hurry.By the end, if it works, the last note will not feel like a finish. It will feel like the room has simply gone quiet.

name: आज रंग है - Aaj Rang Hai
description: Aaj Rang HaiThere is a folk tale in Chishti circles about Amir Khusrau. He goes looking for a guru, finds Nizamuddin Auliya, and what comes out of him isn't a treatise but a song: aaj rang hai, today there is colour. Whether it happened quite like that, no one can say. But the song has been sung at the dargah in Delhi for about seven hundred years, and singers still turn to it when they want to name the moment when searching stops and something simply arrives.This evening's three sets come from three corners of the country, and from three different ways of living with that same question.Gurupriya Atreya and Vedanth Bharadwaj open with Kabir and the other Bhakti poets. Vedanth trained in Carnatic, Hindustani and Western classical music, and for years has sung the saint-poets, Bhakti and Sufi alike. Gurupriya sings with him. These verses were never meant to sit on a page. They were made to be sung among people, and that is how the two of them take them up.Santhi Priya follows with songs of the Bauls. For generations the Bauls of Bengal have been wanderers, singing about the moner manush, the person of the heart, the divine who lives in the body rather than in a temple or a mosque. Santhi Priya learned this music from her guru, Parvathy Baul, and is spoken of as the first woman from Kerala to sing it. A tradition this rooted in Bengal now has a voice from the other end of the country, which says something about how these songs have always moved: on foot, from teacher to student.After a short break, Mir Rajak and Group come to us from Pugal in Rajasthan. They are Mirasis, a hereditary community of musicians whose families have carried the Sufiyana kalam for centuries. In a single sitting they will go from Bulleh Shah and Khwaja Ghulam Farid to the bhajans of Kabir and Meera, without pausing to mark the change. For them there is no border to cross. The labels we bring, Sufi here and Bhakti there, are mostly our own.

name: चलो हमारा देस - Chalo Hamara Des
description: Chalo hamara des, come to my country, is one of Kabir's recurring calls. The country he means is not on any map. It is his name for the place a seeker arrives at when the searching quiets down, and in the oral traditions of Malwa and elsewhere, singers have carried this invitation from village to village for centuries, mostly in the voices of people who never thought of themselves as performers.This workshop takes that call as its starting point. Over four and a half hours, we will learn and sing songs from Kabir, Meerabai and the Sufi kalam, and pay attention to what they are actually saying. Many of these songs begin with ordinary things: a pot, a thread, a well, a lamp, a road. From there they move, sometimes in a single line, towards what cannot be seen or named. We will follow that movement, starting with the familiar and letting the songs take us further in.The poets did not agree on one way of walking this road. Meera longs and waits. Kabir argues, mocks and asks awkward questions. The Sufis speak of remembrance, of surrender, of the beloved. We will spend time with each of these voices, and notice where they meet.You do not need to have sung before. These songs were made to be sung together, by people sitting on the ground, not by trained voices on a stage. What matters here is listening closely and joining in.

name: An Immersive Workshop - Jo Dooba So Paar
description: An immersive workshop with  Artists Vedanth Bharadwaj and Mir Rajak and team , its a musical journey into surrender through the songs of Meerabai, Kabir, and Sufi mystics.Jo Dooba So Paar is an invitation to surrender—to step beyond the instinct to hold on, control, and understand, and to discover what becomes possible when we allow ourselves to be carried by the song.The phrase carries a beautiful paradox. In ordinary life, we learn to keep ourselves afloat—to hold on to certainty, identity, control, and the familiar. But in the songs of mystics, surrender can become another kind of crossing. When the grip loosens, something deeper can reveal itself.Across the Bhakti and Sufi traditions, the language of drowning is not one of defeat. To drown is to let the separate self loosen its grip; to cross is to discover another shore. In this paradox lies the heart of the workshop: perhaps the way across is not through resistance, but through surrender.Through songs, poetry, collective singing and deep listening, we will explore longing, love, devotion, dissolution and the mysterious movement from 'I' towards something larger than oneself.Drawing from Kabir and Meerabai and Sufi saints, the workshop brings together diverse musical traditions that speak, in different voices, of the same inward movement.Sometimes, the shore is found only when we stop trying to stay afloat.Jo Dooba So Paar is an invitation to take that leap: to enter the song deeply enough that, for a moment, there is no need to know where we are going.Perhaps that is the mystery of the mystic's path—the one who dares to drown discovers that the other shore was never far away.No prior experience of singing is required. The emphasis is on listening, participation, voice and the shared experience of letting the song take us somewhere.

name: Philosophy Cafe
description: What is a Philosophy Cafe?This is a group conversation organized by Useful Philosophy, designed to help you spot the weaknesses in your own certainties. It is low-pressure, high-clarity, and strictly "No Guru". We live in times of "winning" arguments, where we lose finding truth and understanding.If you are tired of shouting matches and looking for a space to actually think out loud, join our Philosophy Cafe for an afternoon of philosophical conversations.Bring in your questions to philosophize with the group! We put them to a vote and select the most popular question to discuss in the session.We are ditching spiritual cliches and shallow mantras to dive into the dilemmas of modern life. description: Flight Response is a contemporary jazz-inspired songwriting project led by singer-songwriter and music educator Tanvi Rao, known for her work with Sulk Station and Haiku. The project features a collection of deeply personal original songs written over the last year, bringing together her love of jazz harmony, traditional songwriting, and rhythmic exploration with an adventurous spiritAs both an educator and a lifelong learner, Tanvi believes that artistic growth comes from remaining actively engaged in the creative process. These songs are an extension of her ongoing musical journey, one that has evolved from the electronic and Hindustani influences of her earlier work to its current style—which she sometimes likes to describe as mellow-prog-jazz-pop. Together with Abhin Iype, a pianist and composer whose work bridges different styles of music, Aditya Choudhury, a guitarist and composer, and P H V S D Kiran, a drummer and music educator with an equally curious approach to musical exploration, Flight Response comes to lifeAbout the Artists Tanvi Rao is a Bengaluru-based musician, composer, and music educator. She first gained recognition as one half of the indie-electronic duo Sulk Station, whose debut album Till You Appear received critical acclaim and led to performances at major music festivals in India and abroad. Alongside her artistic practice, she is a committed music educator whose work is grounded in student-led learning, creative collaborations, and community-building. Her work draws on a background in Hindustani classical music, classical piano, contemporary songwriting, and collaborative music-makingAbhin Iype is a pianist, composer and producer from Bangalore, India. Over many years of musical exploration, has developed a unique touch on his instrument, and an engaging and supportive attitude towards listening and interacting with other musicians. Having studied jazz piano at the Conservatory of Maastricht in the Netherlands, he has worked and collaborated with several artists from all over the world including Dimitris Terpizis Quartet, Orchestravian, Henri Schappert, Fransisco Laurito, hagneya, and Fringe Orchestra. Kiran is visiting faculty at R.V. University and teaches at his studio, The Portal. He holds a Trinity Grade 8 distinction and has won the London Sinfonietta’s Steve Reich Clapping Music competition. name: The Working Woman's Hormone Toolkit by Aditi Singh
description: The first Working Woman’s Hormone Toolkit began as a small, intimate circle. This second edition returns by popular demand, with the same content in a bigger room, because many working women have been quietly asking the same question: why does no one teach us how our own hormones actually work?Working women in India are often expected to navigate back-to-back meetings, tight deadlines, limited sleep, and constant stress with little understanding of how hormones can influence energy, mood, focus, and stress tolerance. The Working Woman’s Hormone Toolkit is a hands-on, two-hour workshop designed to bridge that gap with a science-backed, practical approach to understanding the menstrual cycle as a strategic advantage rather than an inconvenience to push through.Participants will leave with a practical toolkit they can apply in their everyday work life, rather than theory that gets forgotten after the session.What’s In The Toolkit?1. Cycle Syncing, DecodedUnderstand the follicular, ovulatory, luteal, and menstrual phases and explore how they can align with different aspects of the workweek, from pitching ideas and deep-focus work to rest and recovery.2. The Hormone-Mood-Energy LinkExplore why energy, mood, and focus can vary across the cycle and understand the role of oestrogen and progesterone.3. Food & Lifestyle LeversDiscover simple, evidence-based adjustments that can support different phases of the cycle, without fad diets, supplement stacks, or restrictive rules.4. Stress ManagementLearn accessible and sustainable techniques to manage chronic workplace stress and support healthier hormonal function.The workshop also includes an interactive conversation with other working women, creating a space to openly discuss the realities of navigating work alongside the menstrual cycle.Grounded in research, translated into accessible language, and designed specifically around the realities of working in India, the session requires no prior knowledge, just curiosity about understanding the body better.Who Is Aditi Singhal?Aditi Singhal founded The Whole Prescription based on her experience navigating two very different worlds: the rigour of Western medical science and the realities of women’s healthcare in India. Her work began with gut health research before expanding into hormonal health, driven by a desire to better understand the gaps in how women learn about and navigate their own health.The Working Woman’s Hormone Toolkit is the workshop she wished she had access to, designed to help women better understand their cycles and make informed choices. She has conducted 200+ workshops across the US, Canada, and Mexico, and brought the first edition of this workshop to Bangalore as a small, intimate circle. This second, larger edition builds on the response to that first session.
